title: Tazria: wait seven days (Leviticus 13:4–6)
hook: when unsure, the priest waits a week and looks again

segments.voice: Yesterday in Tazria, the priest had to come close and look. Your line was look, don't assume. Did you find out one thing for yourself? Today, what the priest does when looking isn't enough. Day three hundred ninety-eight.

An email sent at eleven at night can read very differently at nine the next morning. So can a verdict on someone made on their worst day, before their next week has a chance to prove it wrong. Speed feels like decisiveness. Sometimes it's just impatience wearing a suit. The priest in Leviticus 13 has looked carefully, in good light. And sometimes he still can't tell. The spot is white, but it isn't deeper than the skin. The hair hasn't turned. It could go either way. The Torah tells him exactly what to do with not knowing.
screen: `SENT AT ELEVEN AT NIGHT.` → `THE PRIEST CAN'T TELL.` → `WHAT TO DO WITH NOT KNOWING.`

segments.voice: Here's the instruction. When the signs are unclear, the priest shuts the person away for seven days. The Hebrew verb is hisgir, to shut in or close up. He doesn't declare them unclean. He doesn't declare them clean. He waits. Then comes a second look. On the seventh day the priest looks again. If the spot has spread, now he knows. If it hasn't, he waits another seven days and looks a third time. Only then, if it has faded and stayed put, is the person declared clean, washes their clothes, and goes home. Two weeks, at most, in this passage. The waiting protects two things. A hasty verdict of unclean would send someone outside the camp for nothing. A hasty clean would miss something real. The week is a kindness to both the person and the truth. The Torah builds in time because first looks can be wrong, even an expert's. Pirkei Avot, the sayings of the sages, opens with the chain of tradition from Sinai, and the first advice in it is for judges: be deliberate in judgment. Slow down. The priest with his calendar is a picture of that advice. Not stuck forever in maybe, and not rushing to certainty either. A set time, and then a fresh look. A week is long enough for a lot of things to show what they really are.
screen: `HISGIR: SHUT AWAY SEVEN DAYS.` · `THE SEVENTH DAY: LOOK AGAIN.` · `A KINDNESS TO PERSON AND TRUTH.` · `BE DELIBERATE IN JUDGMENT.` · then, large: `LOOK AGAIN IN A WEEK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wait before one decision. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you've been about to decide quickly. A reply, a purchase, a judgment about someone, a plan to quit something. Ask: is this clear, or am I unsure and pretending not to be? If you're unsure, give it a date, like the priest. Not forever. A week, or even one night. Picture yourself looking again then, with fresh eyes. The bell holds the time.
Tazria. The portion where an unsure priest waits seven days, looks again, and only then decides.
Your line: look again in a week. Today, put one decision you're unsure about on your calendar for seven days from now. Day three hundred ninety-eight.

screen: `DAY 398 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: PRAY FOR THE ONE OUTSIDE.`

howItsDone: Pirkei Avot is traditionally studied on Shabbat afternoons in the summer, and its first advice is to be deliberate in judgment, and Jewish courts traditionally avoid rushing a verdict.

declare them clean, and move on.

fork.reveal: the Torah's answer to uncertainty is a set time and a second look, not a guess.

original.note: Hebrew: "seven days": the waiting period before the priest looks again.

trapdoor: what it means: when you can't tell yet, set a time and look again, instead of guessing.
what a scholar hears: the Mishnah calls a person in this waiting period musgar, shut in (Megillah 1:7); the maximum for a skin case is two weeks before a ruling (13:4–6).

notes: Summary of Lev 13:4–6 (two seven-day periods; clean if faded and not spread; washes clothes) is paraphrased; confirm.
Hesger as modern Hebrew 'quarantine/closure' from the root s-g-r: confirm usage.
Pirkei Avot 1:1 'be deliberate in judgment' (havu metunim ba-din) paraphrased; Avot is traditionally studied on Shabbat afternoons in summer; confirm howItsDone.
